title: The staff and the termite
hook: Sulayman dies leaning on his staff, and only a termite eating it reveals his death to the jinn (34:14)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mountains sang with Dawud, and your line was the mountains sang along. Today, his son. Did any piece of work get your full care? Day five hundred forty-four.

A king stands leaning on his staff, watching his workers. They are jinn, beings of smokeless fire, building for him: high halls, statues, basins like wells. They work hard, because he's watching. Time passes. He doesn't move. They keep working. And then something tiny, something none of them noticed, finishes its own quiet job inside the wood. The staff gives way. The king falls. He had been dead the whole time. This is Sulayman, son of Dawud, and one of the Qur'an's quietest death scenes.
screen: `HE HAD BEEN DEAD THE WHOLE TIME.`

segments.voice: Surah Saba', verse fourteen. Pickthall: "nothing showed his death to them save a creeping creature of the earth which gnawed away his staff." The Arabic is dabbat al-ard, a creature of the earth. The verse doesn't name the species. Commentators understand a woodworm or termite, the kind of thing that eats a staff from the inside, and that's where today's title comes from. How long Sulayman stood there, the Qur'an doesn't say. Some commentators guess a long while; the text is silent. Then the point of the verse: when he fell, the jinn saw clearly that if they had known the unseen, they wouldn't have kept on in humiliating toil. Here's why that stings. Commentators explain that jinn were thought to know hidden things, and fortune-tellers claimed their help. And here are the jinn, working at full speed for a master who can't see them, fooled by a man leaning on a stick. The only one who knew was a small creature chewing wood. So the verse quietly takes the air out of a big claim. In the Qur'an, the unseen, al-ghayb, belongs to Allah. Not to jinn, not to kings, not to anyone with a reputation for secret knowledge. And there's a second, gentler point. Sulayman, who had armies and wind and jinn at his command, died as everyone dies, here standing up, in the middle of an ordinary day. All that power, and his death was found out by a termite. The verse doesn't mock him. It just tells the truth about how little anyone knows.
screen: `A CREATURE OF THE EARTH, EATING THE STAFF.`

segments.voice: The practice: notice how little anyone knows. Sit still. Think of the people you'll see today. Pick one, and quietly list what you actually don't know about them: what they're carrying, what they're afraid of, what happened this morning. Let the list get long. Then notice how much of your day runs on guesses. If you'd like, rest in the verse's idea: what's unseen is held by Someone, not by us. The bell holds the time.
The staff and the termite. Sulayman's death, unnoticed by the jinn, shown only by a creature of the earth eating his staff. Today's word.
screen: `THE STAFF AND THE TERMITE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: only the termite knew. Today, when someone sounds sure about what's really going on, theirs or yours, remember the jinn working for a king who wasn't watching. Day five hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims believe knowledge of the unseen (al-ghayb) belongs to Allah alone, and many scholars cite this verse when warning against fortune-telling and claims that jinn reveal hidden things.

myth: the Qur'an names the creature a termite
it says a creature of the earth; commentators understand a woodworm or termite.
the Qur'an says how long Sulayman stood dead
the text is silent; any length is a commentator's guess.
the verse shows the jinn didn't know the unseen
if they had, they wouldn't have kept toiling for a dead king.

fork.setup: you're one of the jinn, building for Sulayman. he stands over you, leaning on his staff, day after day. what do you do?
fork.reveal: they kept working. only when a creature ate through the staff and he fell did they realize they didn't know the unseen.

original.note: Arabic: a creature of the earth, the small thing that gnawed Sulayman's staff.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strange story about a bug.
what it means: a king's death goes unnoticed by beings thought to know secrets, and a small creature reveals it.
what a scholar hears: 34:14 answers the belief that jinn know al-ghayb; the staff is minsa'ah, and dabbat al-ard is left unnamed by the text.

sources.quoted: nothing showed his death to them save a creeping creature of the earth which gnawed away his staff.

sources.ref: classical tafsir on 34:14 (the creature as woodworm or termite)

notes: Pickthall wording of 34:14 quoted from memory; please confirm.
The jinn are described as 'beings of smokeless fire' (55:15) in the hook; confirm phrasing.
The claim that jinn were popularly thought to know hidden things, and that this verse answers it, follows common tafsir; confirm.
Duration of Sulayman standing is left unstated, as the Qur'an is silent; some tafsir give a year.

Editor review 2026-10-01: the hook's 'days pass' contradicted the teach's 'the text is silent' on how long, now 'time passes'; cut the superlative 'the strangest death scene'; 'basins as wide as reservoirs' brought back to the text's 'like wells'; 'most commentators' softened; the claim about jinn and fortune-tellers attributed to commentators; the unseen belonging to Allah framed as the Qur'an's teaching; fixed the garbled 'died like anyone does, standing up'.
